extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and educated readers evaluating or producing poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_short: literary criticism of poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for assessing poetic style, dramatic characterization, narrative structure, description, and literary integrity in 19th-century (and general) poetic and dramatic writing. Emphasizes what makes passages effective in context and what counts as faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid meretricious ornament; value ruggedness with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: In their hatred of meretricious ornament, and of what Cowper calls “creamy smoothness,” they erred on the opposite side. Their style was too austere, their versification too harsh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject superficial, sugary ornamentation ('creamy smoothness'), but do not swing to the opposite extreme of excess austerity or harshness; balance vigor and restraint. The essay credits the rugged school with valuable service while warning that their versification could be 'too harsh.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic character: avoid constructing personified epigrams or sharp antitheses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by rejecting what is natural that satirists and historians produce these striking characters... If the dramatist attempts to create a being answering to one of these descriptions, he fails, because he reverses an imperfect analytical process. He produces, not a man, but a personified epigram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble characters by piling up contradictory traits for effect (satirical/antithetical sketches). Instead, create unified, believable human beings whose contradictions arise naturally, not as the result of judicious exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show characters through action and speech, do not tell or analyse them
rubrics_metrics.description: He analysed them; he made them analyse themselves; but he did not make them show themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exposition that 'tells' the reader what a character is like. Great dramatists let characters reveal themselves by what they do and say; avoid flat summaries of temperament or having characters 'analyse themselves' in place of lived behavior. Examples of the anti-pattern: Byron often 'made them analyse themselves' rather than making them act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must be genuine conversation, not disguised soliloquy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is curious to observe the tendency which the dialogue of Lord Byron always has to lose its character of a dialogue, and to become soliloquy... The other interlocutors are nothing more than good listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all speakers in a scene contribute materially; interlocutors should prompt, resist, and develop the scene rather than serving merely as foils for one character's long monologue. The scene should feel like interaction, not an extended single mind speaking through many mouths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic speeches must owe interest to character and situation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing dramatic in these speeches, that they derive none of their effect from the character or situation of the speaker, and that they would have been as fine, or finer, if they had been published as fragments of blank verse by Lord Byron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'fine' speech in drama should gain much of its power from its placement, speaker, and dramatic circumstances; otherwise it risks being merely lyrical prose that could be detached as an extract without loss. The worst case is beautiful lines that are irrelevant to the play's action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative poems require a coherent plan and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: His two longest works, Childe Harold and Don Juan, have no plan whatever. Either of them might have been extended to any length, or cut short at any point... collections of fragments; and, though there may be no empty spaces marked by asterisks, it is still easy to perceive, by the clumsiness of the joining, where the parts for the sake of which the whole was composed end and begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid composing extended narratives as loose collections of fine passages. Plot and arrangement should be deliberate so that the whole feels coherent rather than a stitched-together sequence of brilliant but disconnected fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: favour economy, rapidity, and bold selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Description... rapid, sketchy, full of vigour; the selection happy, the strokes few and bold. The proverb of old Hesiod, that half is often more than the whole, is eminently applicable to description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, striking images over minute, exhaustive inventories. Select salient details, sketch them vividly, and avoid prolix exactitude, which can diminish effect. 'Half is often more than the whole'—brevity can enhance impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infuse description with feeling; let perception be personal
rubrics_metrics.description: His descriptions, great as was their intrinsic merit, derived their principal interest from the feeling which always mingled with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive passages gain power when they are interwoven with the speaker's feeling or perspective; description should not be cold cataloguing but should reveal emotional relation to the scene or object. Example: Byron's landscapes are valuable because they are accessories to a central, felt figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive authorial egotism and self-insertion
rubrics_metrics.description: He was himself the beginning, the middle, and the end, of all his own poetry... all were mere accessories, the background to one dark and melancholy figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist making the author (or a single persona) the constant focal point of every scene and description. Overuse of a self-portrait persona reduces variety and can make works feel narcissistic rather than universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary emotional palette; avoid monotonous repetition of a single mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Never had any writer so vast a command of the whole eloquence of scorn, misanthropy, and despair... Never was there such variety in monotony as that of Byron. Year after year... he continued to repeat that to be wretched is the destiny of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a particular affect (e.g., melancholy) is powerful, rely on a range of tones and emotions across a writer's oeuvre to avoid tedium and diminishing returns. Repeating a single sentiment exhaustively lessens its force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create genuinely distinct characters rather than situational variants
rubrics_metrics.description: His women, like his men, are all of one breed. Haidee is a half-savage and girlish Julia; Julia is a civilised and matronly Haidee... Yet the difference is a difference of situation only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate characters by temperament, motive, and inner life, not merely by external circumstances. Avoid reusing the same archetypal temperament in different costumes or situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatist should not model characters on satirical or historiographical caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the business of the dramatist to exhibit characters in this sharp antithetical way... By judicious selection and judicious exaggeration, the intellect and the disposition of any human being might be described as being made up of nothing but startling contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and historical epigrammatic sketches have uses, but their sharp-contrast method produces figures unsuitable for drama, where naturalism and psychological coherence are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be enslaved by rigid classical unities
rubrics_metrics.description: He has distinctly declared his approbation of the unities, the most absurd laws by which genius was ever held in servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid adherence to formal rules (e.g., strict classical unities) can stifle genius and natural dramatic effect; use form to serve dramatic truth rather than obey arbitrary servitude to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor perspicuity, energy, and conciseness for broader impact
rubrics_metrics.description: What Mr. Wordsworth had said like a recluse, Lord Byron said like a man of the world, with less profound feeling, but with more perspicuity, energy, and conciseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal includes wider readership or exoteric appeal, prioritize clarity, force, and economy in expression. Dense or mysterious style may be profound but less likely to secure general sympathy or popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary integrity: resist patronage, puffing, and manufactured praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is now the patron, and a most liberal patron. ... They formerly used flattery. They now use puffing. ... The puffing of books is now so shamefully and so successfully carried on that it is the duty of all who are anxious for the purity of the national taste, or for the honour of the literary character, to join in discountenancing the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid participating in or relying on artificial promotional practices (puffing, collusive eulogies, paid panegyrics) and don’t prostitute literary praise for pecuniary gain. Maintain independence from flattering patrons and manufactured publicity; value dignity and authenticity in literary reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek authenticity in persona and sentiment; avoid theatrical affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: How much of this morbid feeling sprang from an original disease of the mind, how much from real misfortune, how much from the nervousness of dissipation, how much was fanciful, how much was merely affected, it is impossible for us... Whether there ever existed, or can ever exist, a person answering to the description which he gave of himself may be doubted; but that he was not such a person is beyond all doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the voice and attitudes adopted in poetry and prose have an internal plausibility and integrity. A façade of misanthropy or perpetual suffering that contradicts the author's behavior will ring false and diminish credibility.
